Ukraine: nearly 1,200 drones launched at Russia in one night, 467 of them at Moscow, as the Kremlin stalls Europe's arrival at the table

On the night of November 12 to 13, Ukraine carried out one of its largest air attacks of the war: Russia says it shot down 1,198 drones, 467 of them over Moscow. Russia responded with 117 drones. At the same time, Moscow denies having agreed to invite the Europeans to the negotiations [1][2][4].

The Russian Defense Ministry says it intercepted 1,198 long-range Ukrainian drones over more than 15 regions [1]. The AP news agency describes it as one of the largest Ukrainian air attacks since the start of the war [2].
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin counted 467 drones targeting the capital, according to the RIA Novosti agency [1]. Flights were suspended at airports in the region [3].

According to Russian authorities, the strikes killed seven people, including a 12-year-old child, and injured 17 people in three regions [2]. In Volgograd, in the south of the country, four people died in an industrial zone that was hit, according to the governor [1].

On the other side, the Ukrainian air force counted 117 Russian drones, 63 of them jet-powered, which killed at least two people, including a 17-year-old [2]. In Kyiv, a hospital was hit around 3 a.m.: the building was badly damaged and one person was injured [1].

Volodymyr Zelensky says restrictions applied over the occupied territories and along the front line cap his interceptor drones at about 160 km/h, making it “impossible” to hunt Russia's much faster jet-powered Shaheds [2].

On the diplomatic front, US envoy Jared Kushner says Vladimir Putin has agreed to involve Europe in the negotiations; the Kremlin has not confirmed this [1]. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova says the issue was “not discussed” in Moscow with Kushner and Steve Witkoff [4].

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov will only consider widening the format if the Europeans show they truly want to contribute to peace; adviser Yuri Ushakov is asking them to choose between “peace” and “war” [4].

Key takeaway: both sides are negotiating while striking harder and harder, and Ukraine is showing it can hit the heart of Russia en masse, including its capital and industrial zones, just as it is being decided who will sit at the table [1][2].

Ukrainian drones also serve as economic leverage: by targeting industrial sites such as in Volgograd and paralyzing Moscow's airports, Kyiv is making the Russian economy pay for the war without waiting for the outcome of the talks [1][3]. Finland also says Ukraine struck a Russian warship near its coast during the Abu Dhabi talks; Moscow has not commented [5].

On substance, nothing is moving: Russia still demands all of Donbas, and Abu Dhabi produced only a large prisoner exchange [1]. The same day, EU leaders chose their team of negotiators, but Moscow is demanding an end to European military aid [4].
For you, this escalation weighs on European military spending, and therefore on public budgets, including in France, one of the five countries chosen to represent Europe.
In the coming weeks
Prisoner exchange planned under the Abu Dhabi agreement, and the next round of negotiations, with European participation still disputed by Moscow [1][4].

China: more than $3 billion in data centers bank on Nvidia chips banned from export, Reuters reveals

By combing through more than 150 tenders and contracts, the Reuters news agency identified at least 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion) worth of AI projects in China built on Nvidia chips that Washington bans from export. The investigation, published on November 13, comes the day after Jensen Huang's resignation [1][2].
Reuters analyzed more than 150 public procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and Chinese company documents. Total: more than 23 billion yuan, or $3.2 billion [1][2].
The projects target Nvidia's H100, H200 and H800 chips [1]. Yet Nvidia says US export controls have effectively driven it out of China's AI data center market [1][4].

In Fujian province, a 6.2 billion yuan ($873 million) computing center planned in Xianyou county requires H100 chips and is seeking partners [2]. In Shaanxi, a subsidiary of the state-owned group Sinomach won a 3 billion yuan contract for a center equipped with H100s and H200s [2].

In Inner Mongolia, a 1.5 billion yuan project plans 625 H200 servers [2]. In Gansu, a 1.16 billion yuan construction contract was awarded in July, though the documents do not prove the chips were delivered [2].
Some sites are already running: the city of Wuxi, in Jiangsu, announced in March 2025 the launch of a computing cluster equipped with H800 chips [2].
Since January, the Trump administration has been reviewing H200 export licenses case by case for Chinese customers deemed eligible [1].

Jensen Huang resigned as head of Nvidia on Thursday after allegations targeting Alice Huang, a former executive linked to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner [1][3]. Megaspeed denies illegally diverting chips to China. According to Reuters, the projects identified have no established link to Megaspeed, and nothing publicly shows that Jensen Huang violated export rules [1][3].
Key takeaway: despite US bans, Nvidia's most powerful chips remain at the heart of China's AI boom, from the big coastal cities to remote western provinces [2].

The scandal around Jensen Huang changes the picture. A US intelligence memo reportedly concluded that China's Ministry of State Security had recruited the Chinese executive to gather information on Nvidia and its boss; the Chinese embassy calls these reports “groundless” [6]. Huang had openly argued for loosening export controls [2].
According to analysts and lawyers quoted by the South China Morning Post, the affair could weaken Nvidia's lobbying against these controls and lead to stricter limits on sales to China [5].
For Chinese operators, the risk is real: delays, supply disruptions or costly redesigns around Chinese chips if Washington tightens the screws [2].

For you, this is a battle shaping the global AI race. If Washington tightens the rules further, Nvidia loses access to part of Chinese demand, and index funds heavily exposed to the chip giant, often found in French people's savings, may feel the shocks.

Japan: Sanae Takaichi will go to China for the first time, a year after the Taiwan crisis, but Beijing still refuses to talk to her

Tokyo announced on Friday, November 13, that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will travel to the Philippines and then China from November 16 to 19, for the ASEAN summit in Manila and the APEC summit in Shenzhen. It is her first visit to China, while Beijing has been shunning her government since her remarks on Taiwan [1][3][4].
The schedule: ASEAN-related meetings in Manila, including a Japan-ASEAN summit, then the APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19 [1][4][7].
This is Sanae Takaichi's first visit to China since taking office [1][3].
According to Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki, she will discuss trade, investment, regional economic integration, economic and energy resilience, and the digital economy [1].
No one-on-one meeting with Xi Jinping has been announced, and analysts consider a meeting very unlikely [1][5]. Beijing refuses any ministerial-level talks with her government [1].

The root of the dispute: on November 7, 2025, before parliament, Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan and justify a military response. Beijing denounced the crossing of a “red line” and “unacceptable interference” [4].
China then advised its citizens to avoid Japan, reinstated its ban on Japanese seafood and imposed export controls on strategic materials such as rare earths [3][4].
On the first anniversary of those remarks, Chinese spokesman Guo Jiakun accused Tokyo of “continuing to dodge” and showing no willingness to correct them, in other words to retract them [4][5].

Key takeaway: the Japanese prime minister will sit at the same table as Xi Jinping, but with no guarantee of speaking to him. The Chinese Foreign Ministry's reaction reinforces the view that a China-Japan summit will not take place [5].

The dispute already has a cost: rare earths under control, Japanese seafood banned again, Chinese tourists told to avoid Japan [3][4]. Rare earths are essential for electric motors and electronics, pillars of Japanese industry. The trip to Shenzhen is therefore also an attempt to reopen economic dialogue, with trade and energy resilience on the agenda [1].

At the same time, Tokyo is rearming. The government is considering about 60 trillion yen in military spending over five years, as part of the revision of its three main security documents by the end of the year. The defense and finance ministries are clashing over the amount and the funding, and Takaichi is reluctant to raise taxes to pay for it [6].

For you, this matters because of rare earths: if China uses them as a weapon against Japan, it can do so against others. European car and electronics manufacturers, which also depend on them, are closely watching this crisis and its effects on component prices.

news.2026-11-14-egypte-terres-mer-rouge-: Egypt: to ease its debt, Cairo pledges land on the Red Sea coast, and the opposition denounces a sell-off

In a decree published this week, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi authorizes the state to use public land on the Red Sea coast not only to issue sukuk, Islamic bonds, but also to directly repay public debt. The Finance Ministry insists the land will not be sold [1][2][3].
Decree No. 448 of 2026 amends a previous text: land until now reserved solely for sovereign sukuk issues can now also be used to reduce public debt [1].

Published figures differ: the Egypt Today website mentions about 2,669 feddans, or 11.2 million square meters, while Daily News Egypt and Forbes Middle East cite 26,690 feddans (the feddan, an Egyptian unit, equals about 4,200 m²) [3][4][6].
According to local media, the land is in Ras Shukeir, a coastal area near Ras Gharib, where the state had already allocated about 174 km² for the same purpose in 2025 [5].

The Finance Ministry specifies that the land “is not being sold”: it serves as collateral for the sukuk, with investors receiving a right of use for the life of the securities, and any sale or transfer is explicitly prohibited [2].
At the same time, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly reviewed the debt reduction target set for 2030 [3].
Opposition groups, in Egypt and abroad, consider Ras Shukeir too strategic and too valuable to be pledged, and accuse Sisi of “selling off” the coast [5].

Key takeaway: heavily indebted Egypt is turning its public land into collateral to borrow more cheaply or repay debt, a sign that its fiscal room for maneuver remains narrow despite solid growth [1][7].

A sukuk works like a bond compliant with Islamic finance: instead of earning interest, investors receive income from a real asset, here the right to use a piece of land. Egypt has issued one internationally only once, in 2023, with a yield close to 11%, a very high cost [5].

In September, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) praised an economy that had “defied expectations,” with growth of 5.0% in the third quarter of fiscal year 2025-2026 [7]. But the decree sets a legal framework, not a costed debt reduction plan, and does not say how much it will bring in [1][5].

What about me? Egypt controls the Suez Canal, a key route between Asia and Europe: its financial health matters for the stability of the whole region and for maritime trade. If your savings go through an emerging-market debt fund, these Egyptian securities may be in it; this mechanism also shows that a state can borrow by pledging its land.

Nvidia posts six straight weeks of losses, its longest streak since 2012, and heads into its first earnings without Jensen Huang on Tuesday

The chip giant fell another 2% or so on Friday, November 13, and lost more than $600 billion in value in one week, after the resignation of its founder Jensen Huang. On Tuesday, November 17, interim CEO Colette Kress will present highly anticipated results [1][2][3].
On Friday, Nvidia lost about 2% and remained one of the biggest drags on the S&P 500 [2]. Over the week, the leadership crisis cost it more than $600 billion in market value, according to the AP [2].
According to CNBC, the stock has just posted six consecutive weekly declines, its longest streak since 2012, and its market value has shrunk by $1.7 trillion over the course of this slide [1].

On Thursday, November 12, Jensen Huang resigned with immediate effect; the stock fell as much as 14% during the session before closing down 4.34% [4]. Colette Kress, its longtime chief financial officer, is serving as interim head [2][4].
The decline spread across the whole sector on Friday: AMD dropped 8.75% and Broadcom 4.8%, after benefiting the day before from investors shifting toward Nvidia's rivals [2][5].
Nvidia will release its third-quarter results, for the quarter ended October 25, on Tuesday, November 17; a conference call is scheduled for 2 p.m. California time (11 p.m. in Paris) [3].
The group said Colette Kress would publish written commentary on the results right after their release, around 1:20 p.m. California time [3].

Key takeaway: Nvidia sells most of the chips that power artificial intelligence (AI). When its stock falls six weeks in a row, the whole AI bet on the stock market is called into question, from Wall Street to Tokyo [1][2].

Jensen Huang's departure creates what markets call a “leadership risk premium”: investors demand a discount as long as they don't know who will steer the strategy. Tuesday's results will show whether orders are holding up regardless [3][4].
The losing streak began before the resignation: on November 5, a massive sell-off in AI stocks had already cost Nvidia nearly 9% in a single session [6].
Nvidia weighs so heavily in indices that its results move index funds around the world, including those held by European savers [2].

For you, Nvidia is probably in your savings without you knowing it: it is one of the largest holdings in global and US index funds, often held in life insurance or savings plans. On Tuesday evening, its results could move these funds one way or the other. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: why a CEO's departure makes a stock fall

A stock's value reflects what investors think the company will earn in the future. When the founder who set the strategy leaves overnight, that future becomes more uncertain: investors demand a discount, and the price falls [4]. The more expensive the stock was relative to current earnings, the steeper the drop can be, because a large part of its price rested on confidence in what comes next. Quarterly results then serve as the deciding test: solid sales and forecasts can reassure, disappointing figures can extend the decline [3]. The money does not necessarily leave the sector: on Thursday, it had moved to AMD and Broadcom, before leaving them on Friday [2][5].
Precedents: the big falls in AI stocks
January 27, 2025
The arrival of the Chinese AI model DeepSeek causes Nvidia to lose nearly 17% and about $593 billion in value in one session, a record for a US company; the Nasdaq falls 3.1% [8].
The previous record, in September 2024, was $279 billion, also for Nvidia [8].
October 29, 2026
Alphabet falls nearly 13%, its worst session since its stock market debut in 2004, wiping out about $500 billion in value, after AI spending deemed too heavy [9].
Doubts about the profitability of AI spending then spread to the whole sector [9][6].
November 5, 2026
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) falls 12.3%, its worst session since March 16, 2020; 28 of the index's 30 stocks are in a bear market [10].
Nvidia loses nearly 9% and turns negative for the year: Jensen Huang's resignation comes on an already fragile market [6].

Copper heads for a fifth weekly decline and hits its lowest since July: the fall in AI stocks raises doubts about data center demand

On Friday, November 13, three-month copper fell 0.5% to $13,519 a ton in London, after hitting its lowest since July 17. It is heading for a fifth consecutive weekly decline, dragged down by the fall in artificial intelligence-related stocks, according to Goldman Sachs [1].
Around 10 a.m. GMT on Friday, three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) was down 0.5% at $13,519 a ton, after dipping to $13,456, its lowest since July 17 [1].
The metal was heading for a weekly decline of about 1.8%, and has fallen every week since mid-October [1].
According to Goldman Sachs, the main driver is volatility in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, which fell after the Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections [1].
The day before, Thursday, November 12, cash copper traded at $13,712 a ton on the LME, and LME warehouse stocks reached 328,600 tons [2].
In China, Shanghai warehouse stocks fell, and the premium paid to import copper at Yangshan hit a seasonal record of $285 a ton on Friday [1].
The decline is sharp compared with the peak of $14,875 a ton reached on September 10, according to the firm BMI [3].
Key takeaway: copper has become a bet on AI. Data centers and the power grids that feed them consume a lot of it; when AI stocks plunge, investors sell the metal too [1].

The decline hurts producing countries: in Chile, the world's largest producer, Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz acknowledged a “technical recession” this week, caused mainly by lower copper output [7][8].
Yet the market is sending mixed signals: the record premium at Yangshan shows that China is still buying physical copper, while funds are selling their futures contracts [1].
US tariffs remain the other unknown: Washington has still not decided on a tariff on refined copper, which already caused huge price gaps in 2025 [3][5].

For you, copper is everywhere: electrical cables, plumbing, electric cars, household appliances. A lower price may, with a lag, reduce the cost of renovation work or equipment, but the effect is slow and diluted. It also weighs on the big mining groups found in commodity funds. How it works: why copper follows AI stocks

The price of copper is set mainly on futures markets, such as the London Metal Exchange, where metal for delivery in three months is bought today [1]. Many buyers are funds that do not want the metal but are betting on future demand. AI data centers and the power grids that feed them consume enormous amounts of copper: when AI stocks fall, these funds fear fewer construction projects and sell their contracts [1]. The physical market may say something else: a high import premium in China shows that factories are still buying metal for immediate delivery [1]. Tariffs add price gaps between the United States and the rest of the world [3][5].
Precedents: copper, a market that surges and falls back
July 8, 2025
US copper (Comex) jumps more than 13% in one session, above $12,445 a ton, a record, after the announcement of a 50% tariff on imported copper [4].
The announcement of a tariff drives up the US price even before it takes effect, as the market anticipates a local shortage [4].
The White House exempts refined copper from the 50% tariff: US copper plunges about 20%, its biggest one-day drop on record, from $5.59 to $4.35 a pound according to ING [5][6].
When the exemption comes, the US premium evaporates at once: copper reacts very strongly to political decisions [5][6].
September 10, 2026
Copper hits a peak of $14,875 a ton, then stays above $14,000 until early November, according to BMI [3].
Two months later, it has fallen below $13,500, with five weeks of declines: AI-driven peaks can unravel quickly [1][3].

The UN Security Council unanimously extended Yemen-related sanctions for one year and demanded an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The rebels immediately claimed new strikes on Saudi oil sites [1][2].
The renewed sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans; the resolution condemns Houthi missile and drone fire on Saudi Arabia and on ships in the Red Sea [1].

The Houthis say they struck the East-West pipeline, an oil site in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh, with no damage reported in the capital [1][2]. The Riyadh-led coalition says it destroyed two ballistic missiles on Wednesday evening [1][2].
The Houthi health ministry says 359 civilians have been killed and 780 injured in the Saudi escalation, a toll that cannot be verified [1].
According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the fighting has displaced 340,000 people [3].
Key takeaway: the war in Yemen, an offshoot of the war against Iran, is targeting the heart of Saudi oil, including the East-West pipeline leading to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea [1][2].
The unanimous vote isolates the Houthis but has not slowed their fire; in Sanaa, they held mass funerals while calling for civilians to be protected [1][4].
What about me? With Hormuz blocked, repeated strikes on the Saudi pipeline threaten another outlet for Gulf oil: enough to weigh on the price of a barrel.
